title: What is sleep, and why do we need it?
citation: Medic, G., Wille, M., & Hemels, M. E. (2017). Short- and long-term health consequences of sleep disruption. Nature and Science of Sleep, 9, 151-161.
content:
What is sleep, and why do we need it?

Good sleep is more than simply spending enough hours in bed. It is a biological process that allows the brain and body to recover, repair, and prepare for the next day. During sleep, the brain strengthens memories, processes emotions, clears waste products, and helps regulate mood, attention, and learning. The body also restores energy, supports the immune system, and repairs tissues. Sleep is a basic requirement for both physical and mental wellbeing.

Isn't 5 hours of sleep enough if I feel fine?

Some people believe they function perfectly well on very little sleep, but most adults need around seven to nine hours each night for optimal health. After several nights of too little sleep, the brain often adapts enough that people stop noticing how tired they feel, even though their concentration, decision making, reaction time, and mood are still affected. Feeling like you are used to it does not necessarily mean your body has had the sleep it needs.

How lack of sleep affects the body and mind.

When you do not get enough quality sleep, the brain has less opportunity to recover and regulate emotions. Stress hormones remain higher, attention becomes more difficult, and the parts of the brain responsible for decision making and emotional control work less efficiently. This is why poor sleep can make everyday challenges feel more overwhelming, increase irritability and anxiety, reduce memory and concentration, and leave the body feeling physically drained.

Why can't I switch off my brain at night?

Many people find that their thoughts become louder as soon as they lie down to sleep. During the day, work, conversations, and activities keep the mind occupied, but at night there are fewer distractions. If you are stressed, worried, or in the habit of thinking through problems in bed, the brain can remain in a state of alertness rather than preparing for sleep. The more effort you put into trying to force yourself to sleep, the more awake you may feel, creating a frustrating cycle.

Trouble sleeping vs insomnia: what's the difference.

Almost everyone has an occasional poor night's sleep because of stress, illness, travel, or an important event. These short periods usually improve once the situation changes. Insomnia is different because sleep difficulties occur regularly, continue over time, and begin to affect daytime functioning. The difference is not simply having one bad night, but experiencing ongoing problems with falling asleep, staying asleep, or waking too early despite having the opportunity to sleep.

Why do I still feel tired after a full night's sleep?

Feeling tired after spending enough hours in bed can happen for several reasons. Sleep quality is just as important as sleep quantity. Frequent awakenings, stress, inconsistent sleep schedules, alcohol, some medications, physical health conditions, or other sleep disorders can all reduce how restorative sleep feels. It is also possible to spend enough time asleep without reaching the deeper stages of sleep that leave you feeling refreshed.

When should I get help for sleep problems?

It is worth seeking support if sleep difficulties continue for several weeks, occur most nights, or regularly affect your energy, mood, concentration, or daily life. Effective treatments are available, including improving sleep habits, addressing factors that keep the brain alert at night, evidence-based psychological therapies, and, where appropriate, medical assessment. Many sleep problems improve once the underlying causes are identified and treated.
